title: George Müller's orphans
hook: a preacher in Bristol cares for orphans and refuses to ask anyone but God for money

segments.voice: Yesterday, Florence Nightingale, who answered her call with night rounds and careful records. Your line was the lamp. Whose long night did you light up? Day nine hundred thirty.

The children are sitting at long tables. The plates are out. The cups are out. There is no breakfast in the house, and no money to buy any. That's how a story told about George Müller begins. He stands, the story says, and gives thanks for the food anyway. Then a knock at the door. A baker, who couldn't sleep, and who felt he should bake bread for the orphans. Then another knock. A milkman, whose cart has broken down right outside, and who would rather give the milk away than let it spoil. Whether every detail happened just so, nobody can check now. But it's the kind of story his life produced. Today, a house full of children run on prayer.

Who was he? George Müller was a German-born preacher who settled in Bristol, in England. By his own account, he had been a wild young man, a liar and a thief, before his faith took hold. In Bristol he saw children with no parents and nowhere to go, and he opened a home for them. Then more homes. Then large orphan houses on a hill outside the city. Here's the strange part, the rule he set himself. He would ask no one for money. No appeals, no debts. He would bring every need to God in prayer and nobody else. He said he wanted the work to show that God hears prayer. He leaned on lines like the one in Philippians, in the King James Bible: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Careful there means anxious. Don't be anxious; ask, and give thanks. And a psalm calls God "A father of the fatherless." Müller took that title at its word. But don't picture a man who skipped the paperwork. He kept careful records of the gifts that came in and the prayers he prayed, and he published accounts of the work. Some readers see those reports as a quiet way of letting donors know what was needed. His supporters say they were thanksgiving, a record of prayers answered. Both are honest readings. What's not in dispute is the rule itself: the children's needs were prayed for, not begged for.

Here's the practice: pray before you ask. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you need to ask someone for. Help with a bill, a favor at work, an apology, a ride. Before you ask, sit with the need itself. Name it plainly. Notice what you're anxious about: the answer, the asking, how you'll look. If you pray, you can bring the need to God first, with thanks, the way Philippians says. If you don't, just hold it quietly and let the anxiety settle a little. Then, when the bell ends, decide whether and how to ask. The bell holds the time.
Müller. The Bristol preacher who opened homes for orphans and asked no one for money, bringing every need to God in prayer alone.
Your line: prayed for, not begged for. Today, before you reach for your phone to ask for something, pause for one breath first, and give thanks for something. Day nine hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Some Christian charities and missions still follow Müller's pattern of making needs known to God in prayer rather than appealing for funds, and his story is told in sermons and classes about prayer.
